title: IS FOLLOWING ADULT INFLUENCERS AFFECTING YOUR SOUL?
paragraphs:
IS FOLLOWING ADULT INFLUENCERS AFFECTING YOUR SOUL?
You Tell Yourself, “I’m Only Looking.” Jesus Asks a Much More Uncomfortable Question: What Is All That Looking Doing to Your Heart?
Nobody heard the click.
Nobody saw the follow.
Nobody knows what appears on your screen when the room gets quiet.
And maybe that is exactly why this conversation is so uncomfortable.
Because some battles do not leave receipts on the kitchen table. They leave fingerprints on the heart.
You can love Jesus and still be fighting something you are ashamed to admit.
You can worship on Sunday and scroll through temptation on Monday.
You can know Bible verses, love your family, serve at church, encourage other people, and still have a private digital world you desperately hope nobody ever sees.
Maybe it began innocently enough.
One suggested post.
One attractive person.
One profile.
One click.
Then another.
You told yourself you were curious.
Then you followed.
Then the algorithm learned you.
But Jesus does not merely ask what your thumb touched.
He asks what your heart wanted.
That changes everything.
The eyes can become a doorway to the heart.
Job said:
“בְּרִית כָּרַתִּי לְעֵינָי”
Berit karati le'einai.
“I have made a covenant with my eyes.”
That is Job 31:1.
Notice the language.
Not a suggestion.
Not a mood.
A covenant.
Job understood something our culture desperately wants us to forget: what you repeatedly permit your eyes to consume is not necessarily spiritually neutral.
And Jesus takes the issue deeper.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Christ moves from the external command against adultery to the internal territory of desire.
The crucial Greek wording includes:
“πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν”
pros to epithymēsai autēn—
in context, looking at a woman with the purpose or movement of lustful desire toward her.
Jesus says that the person who looks in this way has already committed adultery “ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ”—en tē kardia autou—“in his heart.”
Jesus was not teaching that merely noticing that another human being is physically attractive is identical to adultery.
He was exposing something deeper.
The look that becomes lust.
The gaze that welcomes desire.
The deliberate inward possession of someone who does not belong to you.
Jesus moves the battlefield from merely what your body has done to what your heart is entertaining.
And suddenly the question is no longer:
“Did I physically sleep with somebody?”
The question becomes:
“What am I training my heart to desire?”
That question reaches directly into the phone in your hand.
Because you may never touch the influencer you follow.
You may never meet her.
You may never meet him.
You may never send a message.
You may never commit physical adultery.
But Christianity does not define purity merely as keeping your body out of somebody else's bed.
Jesus cares about the heart.
And that means your private scrolling matters.
Not because the internet is uniquely evil.
Not because every attractive photograph is pornography.
Not because Christians are commanded to become terrified of human beauty.
And not because sexual desire itself is inherently dirty.
God created sexuality.
God created marriage.
God created the human body.
The biblical problem is not that beauty exists.
The problem begins when another human being becomes material for lust.
When a person made in the image of God becomes a product in your imagination.
When following becomes feeding.
When looking becomes lingering.
When lingering becomes fantasizing.
When fantasizing becomes returning.
When returning becomes hiding.
And when hiding becomes a second life.
Maybe nobody knows about yours.
Your spouse may not know.
Your parents may not know.
Your pastor may not know.
Your friends may think you are doing wonderfully.
Your church may know the version of you carrying a Bible.
God knows the version of you holding the phone at 1:17 in the morning.
And here is where many Christian messages make a terrible mistake.
They make you feel filthy...
and then leave you filthy.
Jesus does not.
The Gospel does not expose you merely to humiliate you.
Jesus exposes darkness because He intends to bring people into light.
Perhaps you have whispered something like this before:
“God, this is the last time.”
You unfollowed.
Then followed again.
Deleted something.
Downloaded it again.
Repented.
Fell again.
Promised.
Failed.
Cried.
Repeated it.
Eventually, you stopped making promises because breaking them hurt too much.
Now there is a voice telling you:
Look at yourself.
You call yourself a Christian?
After everything God has done for you?
You will never change.
Listen carefully.
Conviction and condemnation do not lead to the same destination.
Biblical conviction brings sin into the light and calls you toward repentance and Christ.
Condemnation tells you to hide from Him.
The Gospel says something astonishing to the person who has sinned sexually, mentally, digitally, secretly, repeatedly.
Come into the light.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
Because Christ's grace is greater.
The same Bible that confronts sexual immorality also announces cleansing.
Paul wrote to the Corinthians about people whose lives had been marked by serious sexual and other sins, and then gave three extraordinary words:
“But you were washed...”
“But you were sanctified...”
“But you were justified...”
That is the scandal of grace.
The Gospel is not God pretending sin never happened.
The Gospel is God dealing with sin at the cross.
Jesus Christ did not die for an imaginary, cleaned-up version of you.
He died for sinners.
At Calvary, sin was not excused.
It was judged.
And the Son of God bore the judgment.
Jesus was crucified, buried, and raised, and everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something shame could never manufacture:
forgiveness.
You do not cleanse yourself enough to become worthy of Jesus.
You come to Jesus because you cannot cleanse yourself.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace teaches us to leave what is destroying us.
Jesus does not merely forgive us while encouraging us to keep feeding the chains from which He came to free us.
There are accounts you may need to unfollow.
There are apps you may need to remove.
There may be private browsing habits that need to become accountable.
There may be conversations with a spouse, pastor, mature Christian friend, counselor, or accountability partner that you have postponed because confession feels terrifying.
There may be a phone that needs to stop sleeping beside your bed.
There may be an algorithm you need to retrain.
There may be a screen you need to stop pretending has no influence over you.
That is not legalism.
It can simply be wisdom applied to weakness.
When Scripture says, “Flee sexual immorality,” the command is not “stand beside temptation and demonstrate how spiritually impressive you are.”
Flee.
Paul connects that command to an extraordinary reality in 1 Corinthians 6:19–20: the believer's body belongs to God, is associated with the indwelling Holy Spirit, and has been “bought with a price.”
Therefore:
glorify God in your body.
Think about that.
Your body is not garbage.
Your sexuality is not garbage.
Your eyes are not garbage.
Your story is not garbage.
Christ does not redeem people so they can learn to hate themselves.
He redeems people so their lives can increasingly belong to Him.
Maybe the question you need to ask tonight is not merely:
“Is following adult influencers technically sinful?”
Perhaps the more revealing questions are:
Why am I following them?
What am I seeking when I open their profiles?
Does this feed lust?
Would I comfortably invite Jesus into this habit?
Would I want my spouse doing exactly what I am doing?
Am I becoming more capable of seeing people as image-bearers of God—or increasingly accustomed to consuming their bodies?
Does this habit strengthen my walk with Christ, or does it repeatedly pull my imagination somewhere I know I should not live?
And perhaps the hardest question:
Why am I fighting so hard to keep something I keep asking God to forgive?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Maybe your finger has already hovered over the unfollow button while your mind began negotiating.
It's not that serious.
Everybody does it.
I'm not hurting anybody.
I can control it.
But freedom sometimes begins with one painfully ordinary act of obedience.
Unfollow.
Delete.
Confess.
Pray.
Walk away.
Then do it again tomorrow if necessary.
Not to purchase God's love.
Not to earn salvation.
Not because Jesus will love you more after you clean up your feed.
But because when grace captures the heart, we begin asking a different question.
Not:
“How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
But:
“How freely can I belong to Jesus?”
And if you fail again?
Run back to Christ.
Do not use grace as permission to surrender to sin, but do not let failure persuade you that the cross has suddenly become unavailable.
Confess.
Repent.
Get up.
Bring the secret into light.
Keep fighting.
Some victories happen instantly.
Others become long stories of sanctification in which Christ teaches us dependence, honesty, discipline, humility, and endurance.
You may have scars.
Jesus still writes redemption stories.
You may have wasted years.
Jesus still writes redemption stories.
You may have damaged trust and now need to patiently rebuild it.
Jesus still writes redemption stories.
You may be reading this immediately after falling into the very thing you promised God you would never do again.
Jesus still writes redemption stories.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build an audience around shame.
To point broken people toward Jesus Christ.
If this article exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But you also do not have to pretend.
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not the only believer fighting in secret.
For a sensitive struggle, sending this privately may be wiser.
Not because an article can keep you pure.
It cannot.
There is probably someone in your circle fighting a battle they will never announce publicly. You do not need to know who they are before you put truth where they can find it.
Supporting Gospel ministry is one practical way believers may steward their resources for Kingdom work.
If you want to support Gospel Warrior and continue walking with this community:
Invite your family.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Invite the believer who is tired of pretending.
Invite the seeker who still has questions.
Invite the person who thinks their past has disqualified them.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending they never struggle.
Because the Gospel is not the story of impressive people rescuing themselves.
It is the story of a holy God saving sinners through Jesus Christ.
And maybe today the greatest act of courage is not pretending you never looked.
Maybe it is finally turning your eyes toward Someone better.
Toward the Christ who knows the search history.
The Christ who knows the fantasy.
The Christ who knows the relapse.
The Christ who knows the shame.
The Christ who knows every hidden room...
and still calls sinners to come into the light.
Repentance says:
I don't want darkness to own me anymore.
Faith says:
Jesus, I cannot save myself.
Grace says:
Come.
And transformation begins when the person who spent years asking, “How much can I hide?” finally begins asking:
“Jesus, how much of me can You have?”
Let Him have the screen.
Let Him have the eyes.
Let Him have the imagination.
Let Him have the sexuality.
Let Him have the secret.
Let Him have the shame.
Let Him have the future.
Because the most dangerous thing on your screen may not be the person you followed.
It may be the lie that whispered you were already too far gone to turn around.
Your secret may explain how you got into the darkness, but the scars in Jesus' hands tell you darkness does not get the final sentence.
